title: Visas, the One-Year Rule and Staying Legal in Georgia
excerpt: Citizens of 94 countries can enter Georgia and stay a full year with no visa, and for a decade the annual 'visa run' was as good as a residence permit. Since 2022 that has stopped being guaranteed: border refusals with no stated reason are documented, overstays now carry entry bans, and the property-permit threshold rose in March 2026. Here is the honest map — visa-free rules, the residence permit routes, the Public Service Hall, the 183-day tax line and the 1% small-business status.
bodyHtml:
One year, no visa — for most of us

Georgia runs one of the loosest entry regimes in the region. Government Ordinance No. 255 of 5 June 2015, still amended as recently as February 2026, lists 94 countries and territories whose citizens 'may enter and stay in Georgia without visa for one full year'. The list covers every EU state, the UK, Norway, Iceland, Switzerland, the USA, Canada, Mexico, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Israel, the Gulf states, Türkiye, Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan and the Central Asian republics. A separate rule lets holders of a valid visa or residence permit from the EU/EFTA, the USA, the UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, Israel, New Zealand or a Gulf state enter for up to 90 days in any 180. ⚠ VERIFY the 90/180 detail on geoconsul.gov.ge before relying on it.

Ordinary passport holders from India, Pakistan, Nigeria, the Philippines, Vietnam and Egypt need a visa; Chinese citizens get 30 days visa-free. Short-stay applicants use the e-visa portal (evisa.gov.ge). The tourism board says a decision on a visa 'is made within 5 to 30 calendar days, depending on the visa category', so don't book flights first.

The visa run — and why it is no longer a sure thing

Because the year runs from each entry, people have long treated Georgia as a place you can live indefinitely by crossing to Armenia or Türkiye once a year and coming straight back. That still works for most people. It has not been guaranteed since 2022. Border police can refuse entry citing 'other cases envisaged by Georgian legislation' with no further explanation, and the refusals have grown: JAMnews reported in August 2025 that Russians are 'increasingly being deported or turned back at the border when trying to reset their stay', with 20 foreigners deported on 5 August and 34 more by 12 August; the Committee to Protect Journalists documented at least six Western journalists refused between October 2024 and June 2025; Kazakhstan has asked Tbilisi to explain refusals of its citizens, and France and Poland issued travel advisories in May 2025. Unpaid fines, a political profile or a passport full of Georgian stamps and no visible income can all be enough.

The overstay trap. Under amendments passed in June 2025 and in force from autumn 2025, overstaying is no longer a fine you pay on the way out. Up to three months over brings an entry ban of six months; three months to a year, two years; over a year, three years — each with a fine that scales, and an unpaid fine blocks any future visa or entry. A register of illegally present foreigners went live on 1 October 2025, and appealing a refusal or deportation no longer suspends it. Count your days from the entry stamp, not from memory.

When you want more than a stamp: the residence permit

A temporary residence permit is what turns you from a tourist into a resident: it gives you a residence card with an 11-digit personal number, the key to banking, a registered lease, an Individual Entrepreneur registration and most online government services. The main routes on the Public Service Development Agency's list: work (employed or running a business; income at least five times the subsistence minimum, and from 1 March 2026 a formal work authorisation must come first, with a transition period to 1 January 2027); study at an accredited institution; family reunification with a permit holder; short-term/property — title to non-agricultural real estate worth at least USD 150,000 by accredited valuation, raised from USD 100,000 on 1 March 2026, with existing holders renewing under the old figure; investment from USD 300,000 with turnover conditions; and a new IT permit (two years' experience, USD 25,000 annual income, three-year validity renewable to twelve). ⚠ VERIFY every threshold at sda.gov.ge before you buy or sign anything — three of them changed in 2025–26.

Apply while you are still legally in the country — the agency asks for the application 40 days before your lawful stay runs out — at any Public Service Hall (the 'Justice House' in Tbilisi and the regional cities), a territorial office, or online at services.sda.gov.ge. Standard processing is 30 days, with paid 20- and 10-day options. Police clearance certificates from home are increasingly requested. Once the permit is granted, collect the residence card, then register your address within one month — it is free, but needs the property owner's written consent.

The tax line at 183 days

Spend 183 days or more in Georgia in any continuous twelve-month period ending in the tax year and you are a Georgian tax resident. Georgia taxes individuals territorially — genuinely foreign-source income (dividends, interest, gains on assets abroad) is generally untaxed — but 'foreign' is about where the work happens, not where the money lands: a freelancer sitting in Vake billing a client in Berlin is earning Georgian-source income. That is why nomads register as an Individual Entrepreneur with Small Business Status at the Revenue Service (rs.ge): 1% of turnover up to GEL 500,000 a year, 3% on anything above, monthly declarations, and the status lapses after two years over the cap. Lawyers, doctors, architects, auditors and consultants are excluded. ⚠ VERIFY the 2026 rules with an accountant — the March 2026 work-authorisation regime also reaches self-employed foreigners, and the rs.ge pages still carry older figures.

The neighbours who arrived in 2022

Say it plainly: since February 2022 Georgia has absorbed a large Russian-speaking arrival. The 2024 census counted 37,715 Russian citizens (26,453 in 2014), 11,542 Ukrainians (1,631) and 4,473 Belarusians (101) among 133,857 foreign residents; The Insider puts the three groups at about 108,000 by 2026. Tbilisi rents doubled year-on-year in May 2022. Many Georgians hold the Russian state, not its émigrés, responsible for the occupied 20% of their country — but the welcome is cooler than the visa regime suggests, and the border refusals above fall hardest on exactly this group.
